about: Diusburg (Duisburg), one port. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/diusburg.md and the spine (Design/content/spine.json). A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what could not be checked. The dossier's warning is kept: in 793 this is a king's estate with a landing, and the market, the church, the Frisians, the palace and the mint come in by eras.

ports.summary: A king's estate on a dry hill above a bend of the Rhine, where the Ruhr comes in and the road east into Saxony, the Hellweg, begins. In 793 it is a landing and not yet a town: barges going down to Dorestad with wine, pots and querns lie a night under the hill, and the king's war with the Saxons comes down the road on foot. A merchant comes for the crossing, for the road and the news it carries, and for whatever the army or the monks up the Ruhr are short of.
ports.seasons: The year runs by the river and the dues: high brown water at Easter, the host on the road east from May, the new wine coming down from Martinmas, and the boats drawn up through the dark weeks to Christmas. The Rhine has no tide here and no bar; the flood silts the foot of the hill each spring.

history.text: From about this year Franks bury their dead in a field south of the hill, and go on doing so into the eighth century.
history.source: Krause, Archäologische Beiträge zur frühen Geschichte Duisburgs (dossier [K-D])

history.text: About this year, some say, a court of the Frankish rulers stands on the hill, a base for the wars against the Saxons. The digs do not prove it so early.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Kaiserpfalz Duisburg', 'Geschichte der Stadt Duisburg'; Krause allows a court only by the late 9th century (dossier [W-Pf][K-Pf]) (?)

history.text: This year the Saxons beyond the Rhine rise again and drive out the priests, and there is hunger in Francia.
history.source: chronicle_793.json (Annales regni Francorum and Annales Laureshamenses 793)

history.text: About this year Liudger founds his house of monks at Werden, a few hours up the Ruhr. This year too the king holds his assembly at Lippeham, where the Lippe meets the Rhine.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Kloster Werden'; chronicle_793.json (ARF 799)

history.text: Liudger dies on 26 March and is buried at Werden.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Kloster Werden' (dossier [W-Werden])

history.text: The emperor musters his host at Lippeham against Godfred of the Danes. His elephant, Abul Abaz, dies there.
history.source: chronicle_793.json 810-summer-elephant-dies (ARF 810; Annales Xantenses 810)

history.text: Danes go up the Rhine. The church at Xanten is burned.
history.source: chronicle_793.json; Annales Xantenses 864 (=863); Krause, Wikinger I (dossier [K-W1])

history.text: A timber well is sunk at the foot of the hill, where a market and a harbour are beginning.
history.source: Krause, Wikinger I: the well's timbers are tree-ring dated 872; market and harbour from the last third of the 9th century (dossier [K-W1][K-D])

history.text: In the winter of this year the Northmen burn Cologne and Bonn.
history.source: chronicle_793.json (Annales Fuldenses 881; Regino 881)

history.text: Northmen who had come from Denmark to Kennemerland sail up the Rhine with Godfrid's consent, take the stronghold of Diusburh, fortify it in their usual way and stay there all winter. Duke Henry camps against them and lets them take no plunder.
history.source: Regino of Prüm, Chronicon, year 884 (ed. Kurze 1890), paraphrased from the Latin

history.text: When spring comes the Northmen burn their camp and go back to the coast. About now the Emperor Charles gives the royal estate to the abbey of Herrieden.
history.source: Regino 884; the grant after Milz, as Krause gives it (dossier [K-Pf]); de.wikipedia puts the grant earlier (?)

history.text: King Arnulf takes the estate back for the crown.
history.source: Milz, as given by Krause, Königpfalz (dossier [K-Pf])

history.text: The abbey of Prüm writes down what it has at Dusburhc: the church, nineteen holdings and two more, and the Frisians who stay there and pay in silver at Martinmas and at Easter.
history.source: Prüm estate book of 893, ch. 97 'De Dusburhc' (Beyer, Mittelrheinisches Urkundenbuch I, 1860, no. 135)

history.text: On 3 August a king's charter names the district of Diuspurch, in the counties of Otto and Eberhard.
history.source: Lacomblet, Urkundenbuch für die Geschichte des Niederrheins I (1840) no. 83

history.text: By about this year the court on the hill has been rebuilt as a palace: a hall, a church, and a closed ring of stone houses with cellars. In these years, or about the year 1000, the Rhine breaks through its bend and leaves the place on a side arm.
history.source: Krause, Königpfalz (dossier [K-Pf]); de.wikipedia 'Geschichte der Stadt Duisburg' has the river move about 1000 (?)

history.text: A synod here puts out of the Church the men who blinded Bishop Benno of Metz.
history.source: Continuation of Regino, year 927 (=929) (ed. Kurze 1890)

history.text: On the Rogation days, 12 to 14 May, King Otto holds an assembly of Lotharingians and Franks here. Two bishops accused of disloyalty are cleared, and the clergy of Maastricht carry the body of Saint Servatius before the king to complain of Count Immo.
history.source: Continuation of Regino, year 944 (=945)

history.text: On 1 March the Emperor Otto gives an estate to the nuns of Essen. His clerk dates it 'at Diuspargum, which we commonly call Diusburg'.
history.source: Lacomblet I no. 109

history.text: King Henry waits here for the slow Lotharingians. The bishops of Liège and Cambrai come first; the archbishop of Cologne comes late.
history.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon V.20 (ed. Kurze 1889), paraphrased

history.text: On 6 December the Emperor Henry, here, gives two estates to the abbey of Burtscheid. After this year, or about 1011, he gives Duisburg and Kaiserswerth to the Count Palatine Ezzo.
history.source: Lacomblet I no. 149; de.wikipedia 'Ezzonen'; en.wikipedia 'Ezzo, Count Palatine of Lotharingia' (the year of the gift is not sure (?))

history.text: From about this year pennies are struck here in the king's name, on the Cologne pattern: Conrad's, then Henry's, then the young Henry's.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Geschichte der Stadt Duisburg' (pieces of Conrad II, Henry III and Henry IV survive); Krause, Duisburger Hafen im Mittelalter (dossier [W-G][K-H])

history.text: Otto, Ezzo's son, gives Duisburg and Kaiserswerth back to the king and is made duke of Swabia.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Ezzonen'

history.text: About now the toll list of Koblenz is set: a ship of Duisburg gives a cake of wax and a pennyworth of wine, a ship of Cologne four pennies and wine; a bought slave pays four pennies, and a seller of swords gives every tenth sword.
history.source: Koblenz toll, in a diploma dated 1104 (Beyer I no. 409); dated to the mid 11th century by Krause (dossier [KZ][K-H])

history.text: On 16 October King Henry gives 'our court called Tusburch' in the Ruhrgau, with its mints, its tolls and the forest between Rhine, Ruhr and Düssel, to Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg and Bremen.
history.source: Lacomblet I no. 205

history.text: Adalbert falls from the king's side. What becomes of his gift is not known.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Adalbert von Bremen' (the gift's fate not checked (?))

eras.text: A king's estate and a landing. Timber halls and barns on the hill with no wall round them, a row of boats on the mud below, an ale-house, a smith and a ferry. The war is a day's walk east: the host goes up the Hellweg in May and comes down it in autumn with hostages and cattle. Nobody here is a count; a steward answers for everything.

The same place with a new neighbour. Liudger has a house of monks at Werden up the Ruhr and passes through with books, masons and questions. The king's assemblies at Lippeham in 799 and 810 fill the river with boats. After 804 the Saxon war is over and the last deported families go by; the steward's men turn to searching eastbound packs for blades.

Quiet. The road east is a road for salt, cattle and monks now, not for the host. Werden grows and sends down for wine, wax and calfskin. The estate pays its dues at Christmas and Easter and the barges go by in the stream without stopping unless the wind makes them.

The Danes have been up the Rhine and everybody has seen the smoke of Xanten. All the same there is more trade than before: a market at the foot of the hill beside the landing, a timber well dug in 872, boats lying round to the Ruhr mouth, and the first Frisians who stay. When Cologne burns in the winter of 881 people begin to bury things.

The Northmen's winter. They come up in autumn, take the place and wall themselves in. The houses burn; the dead are buried in haste. Duke Henry lies in camp at the Ruhr crossing and lets nothing in or out. In spring they fire their own camp and row away downstream.

Building. The court on the hill is laid out new as a palace, with a ditch on the east side, a hall, the Saviour's church and stone houses with cellars. The abbey of Prüm holds the church and nineteen holdings; its Frisians pay it silver at Martinmas and Easter and trade under its freedom from toll. A causeway is laid from the river to the gate.

A king's house. Henry, the three Ottos and the second Henry hold court here sixteen times and more, with bishops, dukes and their horses, and the market eats well in those weeks and waits in the others. A rampart and ditch go round the settlement. Some time in these years the Rhine breaks through its bend and the landing is on a quiet side arm.

The Count Palatine's, and then the king's again. Ezzo's house holds the place until 1045. Pennies are struck here with the king's name, and they travel: Duisburg men are known by their tariff at Koblenz, a cake of wax and a pennyworth of wine. In 1065 the boy king gives court, mint, toll and forest to the archbishop of Bremen, who falls from the king's side within the year.

sites.name: The bank under the hill
sites.see: A long curve of brown mud and gravel under a steep green hill, eight or ten flat barges and dugouts drawn up bow first, the wide Rhine running hard on the outside of the bend. Wet rope, river weed and wood smoke; men shout from the towpath to the boats. Behind, the thatch of the king's barns shows over the edge of the hill.
sites.source: The Rhine ran in a bend right under the hill; boats lay on the bank below it and probably round to the Ruhr mouth (Krause, dossier [K-AM][K-D][K-H]). A harbour is proved only from about 870; a toll is first named in 1065 (Lacomblet I no. 205): a landing due to the steward before that is a guess (?)

sites.name: The king's court on the hill
sites.see: On top of the spur, five men's height above the water: a long timber hall with a shingled roof, barns, a byre and a fenced yard with geese in it, and no wall round any of it in the early years. After the Northmen's winter it is built again in grey tuff: a ring of stone houses with cellars, a gate, a hall for a king. From the yard you see the Rhine both ways and the Ruhr coming in from the east.
sites.source: A flood-free spur about 8 m above the bank; the court unfortified in the 9th century, rebuilt after 883/84 as a palace with a closed ring of tuff houses, finished in the first third of the 10th century (Krause, Königpfalz and Wikinger I, dossier [K-Pf][K-W1]). That a court stood here in 793 is likely, not proved

sites.name: The old grave field
sites.see: A sandy field south of the hill, rough grass over low rows of graves, the oldest sunk and the newest still mounded. A wooden cross as tall as a man stands at the east end, grey with weather. On feast days a priest from the island monastery upriver says Mass here in the open, and the estate's people stand in the wind with their hoods up.
sites.source: The Frankish grave field, about 450 into the 8th century (Krause, dossier [K-D]). The cross and the visiting priest from Saint Suitbert's at Kaiserswerth are invented: no church or priest is attested here before 893

sites.name: The Saviour's church
sites.see: A small wooden chapel inside the court yard, tarred against the rain, one bell under a little roof of its own. After the rebuilding it is a hall church of stone beside the king's hall, and in the last years a taller one that the moneyers put on the pennies. Inside it is dark and smells of wax and damp cloaks; one lamp burns before the altar.
sites.source: The church of the Saviour, first named in 893 and owing Prüm 30 shillings a year (Prüm estate book ch. 97); a wooden chapel at the court proved by digging, a stone palace church in the 11th century (de.wikipedia 'Salvatorkirche (Duisburg)'). The opening year 860 is a guess (?)

sites.name: The head of the Hellweg
sites.see: Where the track from the landing climbs past the hill and turns east, a worn hollow road wide enough for two carts, going off between oaks toward the Ruhr ford and Saxony. A hurdle across it and two of the steward's men with spears; ox dung, dust in summer, deep mud by Martinmas. Whoever comes down it is tired, and whatever they know is three days old.
sites.source: Diusburg lies at the west end of the Hellweg, the road east, which crosses the Ruhr at Broich (en.wikipedia 'Duisburg'; Krause, Wikinger I). The hurdle and the watch are invented; the search of eastbound goods after 805 is the capitulary of Thionville c. 7 (spine thread swords_north)

sites.name: The Ruhr mouth
sites.see: North of the hill the Ruhr slides into the Rhine, clear brown water into grey, with a line of foam where they meet. A wide flat ferry lies on a gravel spit, a rope and a horn hung on a post. Up the smaller river the banks close in under alder and oak; half a day's poling up it is the ford at Broich, and beyond that, after 799, the monks of Werden.
sites.source: The hill lies between the mouths of the Dickelsbach and the Ruhr; Werden up the Ruhr from 799 (dossier 1). The ferry is the project's ferry_barge (story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_ferry_barge lists diusburg); the ferryman is invented

sites.name: The caulkers' strand
sites.see: A flat stretch of bank below the hill where a barge lies on rollers with her planks open to the light. Two men drive moss into a seam with a mallet and pin it under an iron clamp; a pot of pitch smokes on three stones. Oak chips underfoot, and a stack of long trunks from the king's forest waiting for the adze.
sites.source: Iron clamps that held moss caulking between planks, 9th to 13th century (Krause, Duisburger Hafen im Mittelalter, dossier [K-H]); the king's forest between Rhine, Ruhr and Düssel (Lacomblet I no. 205, of 1065); river barges and expanded logboats built here in the project's tables (story/ships_793.json)

sites.name: The smith by the road
sites.see: A low shed open on one side where the road leaves the landing, black inside, a boy on the bellows and a ring of light on the anvil. Horseshoes, boat nails and hooks hang on the post. In the war years there are spear heads in the quenching trough, and a man who is not a customer sits on the bench by the door and watches who stops.
sites.source: Invented, for the spine's hook (swords_north: the smiths' street at Colonia, 'also at Mogontia and Diusburg, where the king's men watch the road east'). Lance heads and a rider's spur lay in the burn layer of 883/84 (Krause, Wikinger I). Nailed horseshoes are not surely attested north of the Alps before the 9th or 10th century, so a smith who shoes horses in 793 is a guess (?)

sites.name: Gerlind's ale-house
sites.see: A long low house at the top of the landing with a green bush on a pole over the door. Inside, one fire on the floor and the smoke going out through the thatch, benches along both walls, boatmen at one end and road people at the other. It smells of malt, wet wool and onions, and everything said on the river is said here a second time.
sites.source: Invented; an ale-house where a road meets a river needs no source. In later eras it is kept by Gerlind's daughters' daughters under the same bush

sites.name: The market under the hill
sites.see: Wet trodden ground between the bank and the foot of the hill, laid with planks and brushwood, with booths of wattle and a timber-lined well in the middle. Leather workers, bone workers and potters sell beside wine barges; a pig goes for five pennies and is argued over as if it were a horse. After the palace is built a causeway with a drain beside it runs through to the gate.
sites.source: The Alter Markt at the foot of the hill, in use from the last third of the 9th century; wet ground kept wood, leather, bone and plants; the timber well of 872 (Krause, dossier [K-D][K-AM][K-W1]); a pig at 5 d in the Prüm estate book (893); the causeway with its side drain and small stone bridge, early 10th century (Krause, Königpfalz)

sites.name: The Frisians' houses
sites.see: A short row of long houses a little apart from the rest, built the Frisian way with the byre under the same roof and a boat shed at the water end. Bales under tarred cloth, a scale hanging in a doorway, children who speak two tongues. On Saint Martin's eve a man from the abbey of Prüm sits at the first house with a bag and a wax tablet.
sites.source: The Frisians who 'stay' at Dusburhc and pay Prüm 8 ounces at Martinmas and 5 ounces and 12 pence at Easter (Prüm estate book of 893, ch. 97). Where they lived is unknown: not inside the later old town (Krause, dossier [K-D]). The opening year 880 is a guess (?)

sites.name: The old banks on the wooded hill
sites.see: North-east of the landing a wooded hill stands over the Ruhr, with two grassed ramparts running through the trees, older than anyone's grandfather. Herd boys keep pigs in the ditch. In the winter of the Northmen there is fresh earth on the old banks, a palisade, smoke, and long ships drawn up below; in the spring after, only burnt stakes.
sites.source: Two old ramparts on the Kaiserberg, which Krause proposes for the Northmen's fort of 883/84; the fort itself has not been found, and the Ruhr mouth is his other guess (Krause, Wikinger I, dossier [K-W1][K-D]). Duke Henry's camp lay at Broich, at the Ruhr crossing

sites.name: The king's moneyers
sites.see: A stone cellar under one of the houses of the palace ring, with a barred door and a bench under the one window. A man sets a blank on the lower die and another strikes it; the pennies come off bright, with a king's head on one side and on the other, in the last years, a church seen from the water above a wall. A third man weighs every twentieth one.
sites.source: Duisburg pennies of Conrad II (1024-39), Henry III and Henry IV; Henry IV's show a church twice, once from the water above a wall (de.wikipedia 'Geschichte der Stadt Duisburg'; Krause, Königpfalz). Mints and tolls named in 1065 (Lacomblet I no. 205). That the mint lay in a cellar of the ring is invented

people.name: Raginhard
people.trait: The king's steward on the estate: tired, exact, fair by the letter, and ashamed of nothing he has been ordered to do.
people.want: Hulls. Every autumn the host sends more people down the road than he has boats to move, and the order says move them.
people.fear: A count's messenger arriving to count the hostages and finding one short.
people.voice: Flat and short, a Frank's Frankish; numbers first, then the reason, then nothing.
people.looks: About forty-five, lean, clean-shaven but for a long moustache, a blue wool cloak pinned at the right shoulder, a bundle of tally sticks on a thong and a short sword he never touches.
knows: who may cross and who may not
what the host is buying this month and what it pays
the king's orders on arms and on the price of grain
which hostages went upriver and to which lord, if he chooses to say
who holds a plot on the bank and for what due

ties.note: Brunger hates the king's men; Raginhard does not know him and would not remember the village
she answers to him and he answers for her; he has twice not written down a thing she did
drinks her ale, pays at Christmas, and learns from her who is on the road
sold him nothing and helped him with everything; wants a Mass said for his dead wife
the king's arch-chaplain at Colonia sends the orders about the hostages downriver to him
sends a boy up to the priest at Colonia when a column is on the Hellweg, so the bank there is ready
the steward at Colonia counts off every boat and writes to ask about each one short
the count at Dorestad led a levy east and left Raginhard the people to feed
farms the crossing to him year by year for a render and has never once had to ask where the king's horses are
Gundhart of Mogontia sends oats and rye down for the hostage bands; Raginhard pays on the day, and each thinks the other the only honest man on the river
in 810 and 811 a wright on the Scheldt sends up for the king's oak, by the emperor's order; Raginhard sells him every trunk the forest can spare and counts the rafts out himself
two bundles of blades with a Colonia weld lie in the court barn, taken at the hurdle; Raginhard knows the smith's name and cannot yet prove the road

lines.greet: A boat. Good. How many can she carry sitting down, and can you leave tomorrow?
lines.greet_again: You again. You brought back the same number you took. I noticed.
rumour: The host took hostages again beyond the Weser. A third of the men, they say. I am to find benches for them.
The king has set the price of oats, barley, rye and wheat. Sell above it here and I must write your name down.
Nothing made of iron goes east without my leave now. Not a blade, not a mail shirt. Half goes to the man who finds it.
lines.trade: The estate buys salt, iron and rope. The host buys everything and pays late. I pay on the day.
lines.warm: There is a strip of bank above the flood line with nobody's name on it. An ounce at Christmas. Ask me properly and it is yours.
lines.saying: The king gives the order in one breath. I carry it out in forty boats.
lines.farewell: Go well. Count them again at Colonia; they will count them there.

people.source: invented; the office from the Capitulare de villis (the steward, iudex, of a royal estate). No count, reeve or priest is named at Duisburg before 904 (dossier 1). Colonia lies a day up the Rhine from here, so what he sends there goes against the stream

people.name: Liudger
people.trait: A Frisian nobleman's son taught at Utrecht and York: gentle with people, hard on shrines, never without a book.
people.want: Books, a bell and glass for the house of monks he is building on his own land at Werden, up the Ruhr.
people.fear: The Northmen. He dreamed of the sun fleeing over the sea from the north with black cloud behind it, and wept.
people.voice: Plain Frisian with a little of York's English in it; asks before he tells.
people.looks: Near sixty, tall and spare, tonsured, a travel-stained cloak over a priest's tunic, a book satchel on his shoulder and a small bronze cross; he leads his horse down to the ferry.
knows: what a book is worth and where one can be copied
who is priest in each Frisian and west Saxon district
the land up the Ruhr and who sold it to him
what the schools at Traiectum and Eoforwic have in their chests
which of the Saxons were baptised by the vow and which mean it

ties.note: the same person
the same person, six years on from the rising
schooled in his church; sends to him for priests and for the loan of books
Alcuin was his master at York, and writes to him still
the blind singer he healed, who now baptises the dying when priests are driven out
the ferryman poles his books up the Ruhr and has been promised a psalm for each trip
ordained priest at Colonia in 777; Hildebold consecrates him bishop there on 30 March 805 (de.wikipedia 'Hildebold von Köln')

lines.greet: You are the Dorestat house with the small boat. I knew your quay before you did. Can she go up a shallow river?
lines.greet_again: The books came dry. I looked at the bottom of the chest first, forgive me.
rumour: The king was at Lippeham with all his bishops, and then the Pope came to him at Paderborn. A Pope, on the Saxon road.
They have made me bishop at Mimigernaford. I asked to be left with my monks. Nobody heard me.
At York they say the heathen came to the holy island like hornets. I have seen that sky in my sleep.
lines.trade: I need what a house of prayer needs from nothing: a psalter, a gospel book, a bell, glass for one window. I pay in silver, slowly.
lines.warm: When the house stands you will have a bed in it, you and your sons, and your name said at the altar.
lines.saying: A church without books is a barn with a cross on it.
lines.farewell: God keep the boat. I will ask at the ferry whether you passed.

people.source: Liudger, about 742 to 26 March 809: founds Werden about 799, bishop at Mimigernaford 30 March 805, buried at Werden (de.wikipedia 'Kloster Werden'; en.wikipedia 'Ludger'; spine cast.liudger). The dream is in Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri (?). That he crossed at Diusburg is the spine's placing, likely and not attested

people.name: Gerlind
people.trait: Keeps the ale-house at the landing: broad, quick, forgets no face and no debt, and feeds whoever comes down the road first and asks after.
people.want: Malt, salt and good hops; a husband for her daughter who is not a boatman; the truth of every story before anyone else has it.
people.fear: A dry summer and a wet harvest. An army camped within a mile of her brewing vat.
people.voice: Fast and warm, a river Frank's talk, a question at the end of every sentence.
people.looks: About forty, stout, red forearms, a linen head-cloth tied at the back, a grey wool dress girdled high, a wooden dipper hanging from her belt beside the keys.
knows: who is on the road and who is on the river, and for how long
what the steward said last night and what he meant
the price of malt, salt and bread here and at Colonia
which skipper pays his men and which does not
who the Saxon woman at the court really is

ties.note: he drinks on tally and pays at Christmas; she tells him half of what she hears
feeds her on fast days and has never asked what she eats on them
her brother; they have not agreed about their father's boat since he died
she is the one person on the Rhine he will sit beside; she knows why
the alewife under the palace at Noviomagus brews with bog myrtle and says so loudly
the alewife in the tower at Colonia; they send each other malt prices and gossip by the barge men
the alewife on the Frisians' shore at Mogontia, at the top of the same river; a question put to one of them reaches the other by Martinmas, and the answer comes back with the new wine

lines.greet: Sit by the fire end, that is the boat end. You are off the Dorestat boat, are you not? What is bread there?
lines.greet_again: Your bench is free. I kept your mate's cup; he left it and a knife, and I have only the cup.
rumour: Forty came down the road yesterday with their children. Not one spoke. The steward bought every loaf I had.
They say the emperor's great beast died at Lippeham. An elephant. Big as a barn, and it died of our weather.
A man was here asking who takes iron east. I told him the smith shoes horses. Was that wrong?
lines.trade: I buy malt, hops and salt, and I pay in pennies or in keep. A week's lodging for a sack of good malt.
lines.warm: Your Saxon was looking at the road again. Take him up to the court kitchen. Ask for Hathuswith. Say I sent you.
lines.saying: Ale is the same in every tongue. It is the reckoning that needs a translator.
lines.farewell: Come back before Martinmas. I broach the strong one then.

people.source: invented; names of attested Frankish parts (Ger-, -lind). The elephant: chronicle_793.json 810-summer-elephant-dies (her rumour is for 810 and after). Hops in her ale so early are not sure: the first written word of hops in brewing is Adalhard of Corbie's, 822, and goods_793.json has hops from 800 (?)

people.name: Wolfhelm
people.trait: Ferryman at the Ruhr mouth and the only man who will take a loaded boat up the Ruhr: slow, sure, superstitious about the river and right about it.
people.want: The crossing held in his own name, not farmed year by year from the steward; a son who can read the water.
people.fear: The spring flood that moves the gravel bars overnight. Drowning with the king's horses aboard.
people.voice: Slow, with long stops; talks of the Rhine as 'he' and the Ruhr as 'she'.
people.looks: About forty-five, short and very broad, a grey-streaked beard, bare legs brown to the knee, a hooded cape of oiled hide and a pole twice his own height.
knows: every bar and snag from the hill to the ford at Broich and on to Werden
when the Rhine will rise, by the colour of the Ruhr
who crossed, with what, and which way they looked
where the old iron thing lies in the river bed
what the ruins over the water are called

ties.note: his sister; she says the ferry was their father's and half hers
holds the crossing of him for a yearly render, and carries the king's people free
carries his books up the Ruhr for a psalm a trip and has begun to like psalms
the ferryman on the Waal; they trade poles and lies at the Christmas reckoning
she saw what he carried over one night in 795 and has said nothing
poles the priest's books up the Ruhr for a psalm a trip; has learned four psalms and argues with the fifth
takes the potter's widow's seconds from Colonia up the Ruhr to the inland farms and pays her in smoked eels; says a pot with a chip pours the same (?)

lines.greet: Across, or up? Across is a penny for four men. Up her is another matter and we talk first.
lines.greet_again: You kept her off the bar where I said. Most do not listen. Most pay me twice.
rumour: She is running red from the hills. He will be over the lower bank in three days. Move your boat.
The priest has bought the bend at Werden. Good land, bad landing. I told him. He thanked me and bought it.
My pole struck iron in mid-stream again, long as two men. It was old when the Franks came.
lines.trade: I carry. I do not buy. But the monks upriver pay for wine and wax and I know the day they run short.
lines.warm: Bring your boat at first light. I will show you the Ruhr once, slowly. After that she is yours to go up.
lines.saying: The Rhine takes what he wants. The Ruhr only takes what you leave lying.
lines.farewell: Keep to the outside of the bend. He is deep there and honest.

people.source: invented; names of attested Frankish parts. The ferry as a lord's right farmed to a trusted man: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_ferry_barge. What he takes for iron in the river is the lead stock of a Roman anchor, 1.36 m long, found in 1968 (Krause, Römische Ankerfunde); 'long as two men' is his own measure of a thing he has never seen

people.name: Hathuswith
people.trait: A Saxon freeman's daughter from the Weser, given as a hostage in 785 and kept to work in the court kitchen: watchful, proud, with a memory like a tally stick.
people.want: To know which of the people who pass her door are alive a year later. To go home, if there is one.
people.fear: Being sent on upriver, south, where nobody speaks Saxon and nobody would know her name.
people.voice: Low and careful in Frankish; in Saxon, quick and exact, with the names of rivers.
people.looks: About thirty, tall, fair hair braided and bound under a plain cloth, an undyed dress with sleeves rolled, a small wooden cross on a cord worn outside where it can be seen.
knows: every hostage band that has gone by since 785: how many, from which river, to which lord
which of the steward's men can be spoken to
where a boy from the Weser was sent in the year of the great hostage-taking
the words of the vow, and what the old words were
who crossed the Ruhr by night

ties.note: of the same district on the Weser; she knew his mother's name before he gave it
the same man, as he is known at Daventre
he answers for her to the count; she cooks for his table and counts his hostages better than he does
the only Frank who has asked her what she was called at home
she saw him ferry a family over by night and kept it; he brings her eels
the Saxon alewife at Daventre; boatmen carry a word between them twice a year, and neither has seen the other
he taught her the Creed in her own tongue and did not ask her to mean it yet

a boy of thirteen with a split eyebrow on the same road south in 785; after the vow at Colonia she was sent back down to the king's kitchen here and he was sent on south, and she has counted him among the living ever since
the old priest at Colonia read the vow over her band at the crossing; she says he was the only one who looked ashamed
a clerk far up the river who, a boatman told her, writes Saxon names the way Saxons say them; she sent him her count of the bands and he sent back thanks, which no Frank had

lines.greet: You want bread, you ask the cook. You want something else, say it plainly. I have a pot on.
lines.greet_again: Your mate stood in my door a long time last year and asked nothing. Tell him to ask.
rumour: From the Weser, the year of the vow, they took the sons south by boat. To the bishops. Colonia first, then further.
At mid-Lent they are to bring every hostage to Mogontia to be counted. The steward had the letter read twice.
They moved a whole district this autumn, wives and children. The land is given to Franks. There is nothing to go home to.
lines.trade: I have nothing to sell. The kitchen wants salt and a quern that does not shed grit. Speak to the steward.
lines.warm: The boy you mean went upriver with eleven others. He would not answer to the name the priest gave him. I remember that.
lines.saying: A hostage eats at the king's table and counts the doors.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you see the Weser, say its name once for me.

people.source: invented; the name from attested Old Saxon parts (Hathu-, -swith). Hostages of 785 and after, the deportations to 804 and the order to bring hostages to Mainz at mid-Lent about 805: Annales regni Francorum; spine thread saxon_end. That hostages were kept at this estate is the spine's placing

people.name: Thiadward
people.trait: The first of the Frisians to stay: a wine and cloth carrier from the Vlie who built a house here and will not be moved from it by floods, Northmen or the abbot's bag-man.
people.want: His silver back out of the ground. A freedom from toll he can show at Colonia. Sons-in-law with boats.
people.fear: The long ships a second time. That somebody saw where he dug.
people.voice: Dry Frisian; says the worst thing first and the price second.
people.looks: About forty, wiry, a short cropped beard, the Frisians' short striped cloak the Franks laugh at, a folding scale in a leather case at his belt and two fingers missing from the left hand.
knows: wine at Colonia, cloth at the Vlie and what lies between
what the Frisians pay Prüm and what they get for it
who was here in the winter of the Northmen and who was not seen again
where the old well was
which barges are for sale and which are only being talked about

ties.note: the duke's camp bought his grain on a promise in the winter of 883; the duke died before he paid
claims to be of the old Dorestad house, three generations on; the name is the only proof
paid Rorik's toll at Dorestad as a young man and counts it still
a cousin at Daventre, who was burned out the year before Diusburg was
sold wine at the army's camp at Ganda in the winter of 880, once, and knew three of the same faces on the ships that came up the Rhine in 883
carries the count of ships on the lower river up to the archbishop at Mogontia with his wine boats, and has his toll there forgiven for it

lines.greet: Dorestat? There is no Dorestat. There is a sandbank and some sheep. Sit down, kinsman, if that is what you are.
lines.greet_again: You came back up a river the Danes use as a road. Either you are brave or your prices are bad at home.
rumour: Colonia burned and Bonn burned. I have put what I own where fire does not go. Do not ask me where.
Godfrid let them through. He holds Frisia from the emperor and opens the door to his cousins. That is what a grant buys.
The abbot's man came for the Martinmas silver. Eight ounces. I asked what we get. He said: you are not asked for toll.
lines.trade: Wine down, cloth and salt fish up. I buy cloth by the piece and I will know if it is short.
lines.warm: There is a house empty beside mine. Under Prüm's hand you pay the abbot twice a year and the toll man never.
lines.saying: A Frank laughs at a short cloak until he has to row in a long one.
lines.farewell: Go down by daylight. And if you see smoke, it is not a kiln.

people.source: invented; the name of attested Frisian parts (Thiad-, -ward). The Frisians who stay at Dusburhc and their two payments: Prüm estate book of 893 ch. 97; their freedom from toll as Prüm's protected men: Ludwig 1986. The short striped Frisian cloak: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34. Kinship with the spine's Thiadbod is his own claim

people.name: Henry
people.trait: The emperor's best soldier against the Northmen: patient, hard, a man who wins by sitting still across his enemy's road.
people.want: Bread, oats and boats for a camp that must outlast a winter; nothing whatever to reach the fort.
people.fear: His own levies going home for the spring ploughing. A merchant who sells to both camps.
people.voice: Few words, a soldier's; asks one question and waits as long as it takes.
people.looks: A man in his prime, broad, a short dark beard, a mail shirt under a red cloak lined with marten, an iron helm on his saddle bow and mud to the thigh.
knows: how many long ships lie under the fort and how many men
what his camp will pay for grain, and that it will pay
who has been seen rowing to the Northmen by night
what Godfrid was promised at Asselt and what he wants now

ties.note: took the Frisian's grain for the camp on his word
has no trust in a Northman holding a Frankish river, and least of all in Godfrid, who has Rorik's lands after him
the Frisian at Daventre, burned out in 882, brings him word of what moves on the IJssel
the archbishop of Mogontia keeps the upper river while Henry keeps the lid on the fort here; boats pass between them with numbers, not greetings (?)
the men in the fort are the leavings of the army that sat at Ganda and burned Colonia; Henry has been fighting the same faces for four years

lines.greet: You came up past their ships and they let you. Tell me why, and then tell me what is in the boat.
lines.greet_again: The grain was dry and the measure was full. My marshal has your silver.
rumour: They built their fort in the usual way and they sit in it. They went out for cattle twice. They came back with fewer men.
Godfrid gave them leave. The emperor made him a count in Frisia and he keeps the door for thieves.
When the thaw comes they will burn it and go. Men who are winning do not burn their own house.
lines.trade: Grain, oats, salt meat, ale. I pay in the emperor's pennies. Sell to the fort and I will hang you from your own mast.
lines.warm: You did not sell to them, and you could have. I will say your name to the count at Colonia.
lines.saying: A fort is a pot. I do not need to break it. I need to keep the lid on.
lines.farewell: Go upstream. Downstream is theirs until spring.

people.source: Henry, margrave and leader of Charles the Fat's armies against the Northmen, killed before Paris on 28 August 886 (en.wikipedia 'Henry of Franconia'); at Diusburg in the winter of 883/84 (Regino 884). His birth year is not known. The words are invented

people.name: Ezzo
people.trait: Count Palatine of Lotharingia and husband of an emperor's daughter: old, courteous, very rich, and careful that nobody forgets the second thing.
people.want: Stone, glass and relics for the abbey he is founding at Brauweiler; a quiet river; his sons well placed.
people.fear: A new king who remembers that Duisburg was the crown's.
people.voice: Unhurried and exact; speaks of emperors by their Christian names.
people.looks: Over sixty, tall and still straight, white hair cut at the collar, a long dark-green mantle with a gold border, rings on both hands, and a board for the tables game carried behind him by a boy.
knows: what the king's court will want when it comes, and when
who strikes the pennies here and at what weight
the toll lists of the Rhine and who is free of them
the price of tuff, lead and window glass
every marriage between Aachen and the sea

ties.note: the Tiel men say the Count Palatine's stretch of river costs more each year, and say it to the king
the moneyer at Daventre, whose pennies Ezzo's steward takes without weighing
the margrave on the Scheldt, duke in Lotharingia from 1023: two great houses of one duchy, courteous at the emperor's table and nowhere else (?)

lines.greet: A merchant of the old Dorestat line. My wife's grandfather would have known your house. What do you carry?
lines.greet_again: The glass came whole. My abbot counted the panes twice, which is his way of thanking you.
rumour: The Emperor Henry is dead at Grone and the princes meet at Kamba to choose. I shall vote, and then I shall see who won.
The lady Matilda is dead. I am building at Brauweiler so that someone will pray for her every day I cannot.
The king means to strike pennies here in his own name. Cologne's weight, Cologne's look. The archbishop is not pleased.
lines.trade: I buy stone from Andernach, lead, glass, wax and silk. My steward pays. I do not discuss prices; he does little else.
lines.warm: Dine with me. Afterwards we will play at the tables. I should warn you that I once won a wife at it.
lines.saying: An emperor's daughter costs three games. The upkeep is another matter.
lines.farewell: God speed you. Tell them at Koblenz you are a ship of Duisburg; it is cheaper.

people.source: Ezzo, about 955 to 21 May 1034, Count Palatine of Lotharingia; married Matilda, daughter of Otto II (died 1025); given Duisburg and Kaiserswerth after 1016 or about 1011; founded Brauweiler in 1024 (de.wikipedia 'Ezzonen'; en.wikipedia 'Ezzo, Count Palatine of Lotharingia'). That he won Matilda from Otto III at a board game is the Brauweiler foundation legend, not history (?). The election at Kamba, 1024. His words are invented

stories.title: The road of hostages
stories.summary: The Hellweg ends at this bank, and every autumn of the Saxon war it delivers people who did not choose to come: hostages, and after 795 whole families moved off their land. The steward wants hulls to carry them upriver; a woman in the court kitchen has counted every band since 785, and one of them had the mate's brother in it.
stories.picture: Dusk on the bank under the hill: a line of Saxons sitting on the mud with bundles and children, two spearmen, the steward with his tally sticks pointing at a small boat, and a tall man of the boat's crew standing very still.

beats.text: Raginhard needs a boat for twelve hostages to Colonia by the feast. He pays on the day, in pennies, and counts them aboard himself. Brunger will not row unless he is told why.
Gerlind has watched the mate watching the road. She sends the merchant up to the court kitchen with her name for a key.

Hathuswith remembers a band of twelve Weser boys in the year of the vow, sent by boat to the bishops in the south, and one who would not answer to his new name. Brunger has his trail (sets sx_brother_trail).
A family slips the guard on the road and reaches the ferry by night. Wolfhelm will take them over if someone will take them on. Carrying them out of the king's reach sets sx_carried_fugitive.
At the king's crossing whole villages wait on the bank to be moved into Francia, and a priest reads them the vow again. The hostages are counted off the boat. The number must be the steward's number.

What Hathuswith remembers, the clerk Hrotbert at Colonia has written: the roll of 785, with the lord's name beside each boy. The two counts agree. He says so, a little put out, and asks who the woman is.
At mid-Lent the hostages kept in the south are brought in to be counted. The brother is among them, grown, with a Frankish name and a lord who values him (sets sx_brother_found).
The merchant comes back and tells Hathuswith what became of the boy. It is the first time in twenty years anyone has brought her the end of a count.

endings.how: The merchant carried the hostages as ordered, full count, and found the brother by asking openly at Mogontia.
endings.text: The steward gives the house its strip of bank and a word to the count. The brother is alive and will not come home: he has a lord, a wife and a new name. Brunger rows on, quieter than before.
endings.reward: flags sx_brother_trail and sx_brother_found; the work diusburg.work.plot at half its cost; standing with the king's men on the Rhine; Brunger stays

endings.how: The merchant took the family from the ferry and carried them out of the king's reach.
endings.text: Hathuswith hears of it before the steward does. She gives the merchant a name on the Weser that will open doors in Saxony for a generation. If the king's men learn of it, they ask at the next toll.
endings.reward: flag sx_carried_fugitive; standing with the Saxons; Brunger's loyalty is fixed for life; a risk at every Frankish toll until 806

endings.how: The merchant refused the steward's hostages and asked nothing at the kitchen.
endings.text: The steward finds another boat and writes nothing down. Brunger looks at the road every time the boat lies here, and in a hard year he walks up it and does not come back.
endings.reward: no silver and no trail; nothing lost with the steward; the mate may leave the crew after 800

stories.reward: The mate's brother found or his trail closed, a plot on the king's bank or a name in Saxony, and a woman in the court kitchen who tells the house what the road carries

stories.title: Books up the Ruhr
stories.summary: Liudger has bought land in a bend of the Ruhr for a house of monks and has nothing to put in it. He wants a psalter and a gospel book from the schools that trade copies with England, a bell, and glass for one window, and he wants them carried up a shallow river by someone who will keep them out of the bilge.
stories.picture: A dugout poled up a narrow river under alders, a book chest lashed amidships under a hide, the ferryman at the pole, and on the bank ahead a tall priest in a travelling cloak standing among fresh-cut posts.

beats.text: Liudger asks whether the boat can go up a shallow river, and lists what a house of prayer needs from nothing. He has silver from his family's land and pays slowly.

At Mogontia the clerk Otbert has a psalter the school at Saint Alban's can spare, copied from an English one. He will send it down to the Ruhr mouth in a hold he trusts, wrapped as he says, for the price of the skins.
The school at Traiectum will lend a psalter to be copied, on the bishop's word, if it is carried dry both ways. Or a copy can be had at Eoforwic for more silver and a sea crossing.
At Colonia a founder will cast a small bell and the wine house of Liutwin has panes of green window glass, packed in bran. Neither likes a boat. Both like silver by weight.
Wolfhelm shows the Ruhr once, slowly: the bar at the mouth, the snag below Broich, the ford. After that the merchant may go up it without him.
Liudger says Mass at the old cross with the new book open. He asks the merchant's name for the altar, and offers a yearly order for calfskin and wax while the house stands (sets bk_parchment).
After Easter a boat comes up from the north and turns into the Ruhr with a bier under a pall. Liudger is going to Werden to stay. The ferryman takes no fare.

endings.how: The books, the bell and the glass all reached Werden whole.
endings.text: The house has an order from Werden every year until the Northmen's winter, a bed there, and a name said at the altar. The monks elsewhere have heard who carries books dry.
endings.reward: flags bk_carried and bk_parchment; the unlocks diusburg.werden_order and diusburg.ruhr_water; standing with the church along the Rhine

endings.how: The bell and the glass arrived, but the books were spoiled by water or never fetched.
endings.text: Werden has a voice and one green window and no psalter. Liudger thanks the merchant for the half and sends to Traiectum himself for the rest.
endings.reward: silver for the bell and the glass; flag bk_lost if a book was spoiled; the Ruhr stays open to the house; no standing order

endings.how: The merchant sold the bell metal or the glass on the way for a better price.
endings.text: The price is good. Wolfhelm hears of it at the Christmas reckoning and the Ruhr has a bar across it for this boat that it has for no other.
endings.reward: silver, about half again what Liudger would have paid; the church's standing lost at Diusburg and Traiectum; no pilot up the Ruhr

stories.reward: A standing order from Werden for calfskin, wax and wine until the winter of 883, free water up the Ruhr, and the house prayed for by name

stories.title: Blades on the east road
stories.summary: The smith by the road shoes horses, and a man who lodges with him sells Rhineland blades to anyone going where the law says they may not go. After 805 the steward's men search every eastbound pack, and half of what is found goes to the finder. The merchant can carry, can tell, or can look at the river.
stories.picture: The open side of a dark smithy at evening: a bundle of blades without hilts half unwrapped from greased cloth on the bench, a dealer weighing hack-silver on a small scale, and outside in the road a spearman looking the other way.

beats.text: A dealer who asks no questions has a dozen blades from upriver, unhilted, greased and wrapped. He wants silver by weight, not coin, and he wants them gone before the steward's man comes back from his dinner.

The blades are welded at Colonia, behind the hurdles at the quiet end of the smiths' row. Bero, who made them, sends them a day down the river under querns and wants a boat that is seen at Diusburg often enough not to be noticed.
At the smiths' yard at Mogontia a king's man leans on the gatepost and counts who goes in. The road east from the upper river is watched as the Hellweg is; the watchers know each other's lists.
The watch at the hurdle turns out every pack going east. Under a fleece or the ballast stones a bundle is easy to miss, and hard to explain. A found blade costs the whole cargo.
Raginhard, or the steward after him, will pay the finder's half for a name. He does not ask how the merchant comes to know it.
A Frankish blade is worth three times its price in the north. A Dane who buys for a king's hall will take as many as can be brought, and remember who brought them (sets sw_buyer_known).
The dealer has a second bundle, and this time old mail from an abbey's store that the abbey's steward cannot be seen to sell.

endings.how: The merchant carried the blades past the watch and north.
endings.text: The house has a buyer in the north by name and silver by weight. It also has a dealer on the Rhine who knows what it did, and will say so if he is ever taken.
endings.reward: silver, about three times the blades' cost; flags sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known; a second, larger offer; a risk of sw_marked at each search

endings.how: The merchant gave the dealer's name to the steward.
endings.text: The dealer loses his goods, half to the palace and half shared. The merchant's share is paid on the day. No smith between here and Colonia will sell the house so much as a boat nail for a year.
endings.reward: silver, a quarter of the bundle's worth; standing with the king's men; the smiths' street shut to the house for a year

endings.how: The merchant bought nothing and said nothing.
endings.text: The dealer is gone by morning. The smith shoes horses. The man on the bench by the door nods to the merchant next time, which could mean anything.
endings.reward: nothing gained or lost; the offer comes again in a later year

stories.reward: A named buyer in the north and heavy silver, or the finder's half and the king's men's good word

stories.title: The winter of the Northmen
stories.summary: In the autumn of 883 a fleet comes up the Rhine with Godfrid's leave, takes Diusburg and walls itself in for the winter. Duke Henry camps at the Ruhr crossing and lets it take no plunder. A Frisian who has buried his silver in the market well needs a friend with a boat, and both camps need bread.
stories.picture: A winter dawn from the river: burnt house posts under the hill, long ships drawn up below a new palisade on the wooded height, thin smoke, and across the Ruhr the tents and horse lines of a Frankish camp in the frost.

beats.text: Colonia has burned. Thiadward says he has put what he owns where fire does not go, and will not say where. He asks the merchant to be the one who knows, in case he is not there in spring.

The army that will winter here is refitting on the Scheldt at Ganda after its beating at Saucourt. Thiadward, who sold it wine there once, says a man who has seen those hulls planked knows what is coming up the Rhine, and roughly when.

Colonia is rebuilt this year with gates, bars and locks, and the fleet goes by it. What a wall turns aside has to land somewhere: it lands a day downstream, where there is a king's court on a hill and no wall at all.
Smoke downstream, then sails. The market empties in a morning. Thiadward's bag goes down the timber well with a stone on it, and the merchant is shown which side.

The fort stands on the old banks. Duke Henry, across the Ruhr, will pay the emperor's pennies for grain, oats and salt meat. A man from the fort offers more, in broken church silver, for the same sacks.

Archbishop Liutbert at Mogontia wants the count of ships under the fort and will forgive a season's toll for it. He has met some of those crews himself, and asks whether the duke needs oats more than he needs prayers.
At the thaw they burn their own camp and go down to the coast. The place is black: house walls, the well choked with burnt rubble, graves dug in a hurry, one of them for a man as tall as a door.
The well must be dug out to reach what is under the rubble. Thiadward is alive, or his widow is. The bag is where it was put, and only two people ever knew the side.

endings.how: The merchant fed Henry's camp, sold nothing to the fort, and dug the silver out for its owner.
endings.text: The duke says the house's name at Colonia before he dies at Paris. Thiadward gives a tenth of the bag and the empty house beside his own. The Frisians here count the merchant as one of theirs.
endings.reward: silver, a tenth of the hoard; the unlock diusburg.prums_men at no entry cost; the work diusburg.work.frisian_house at half cost; standing with the Franks and the Frisians

endings.how: The merchant sold grain to the fort as well as to the duke.
endings.text: The church silver is heavy and good. In spring a boy who carried sacks tells the duke's marshal. The house is not hanged, because Henry has gone west, but nobody at Diusburg sells it a rope for ten years.
endings.reward: silver, twice the camp's price, in broken plate; standing lost with the Franks on the Rhine; the Frisians' houses shut to the house until 894

endings.how: The merchant dug out the well alone and kept what was in it.
endings.text: It is a good bag: pennies of three kings, an arm ring, a cut dirham. Thiadward, or his widow, looks at the well and then at the merchant and says nothing at all. Frisians talk to Frisians from here to the Vlie.
endings.reward: silver, the whole hoard; standing lost in every Frisian port; the story is told at Daventre before the boat gets there

stories.reward: A house among the Frisians under Prüm's freedom from toll, a duke's good word, and a tenth of a hoard, or all of it and the name that goes with that

stories.title: The bell and the spring
stories.summary: Liudger is buying land up the Ruhr for a house of monks and wants a bell for it, cast at Colonia, and glass for one window. He is gentle with people and hard on shrines, and the old people at the landing say the place is named for a god with a spring under the hill, which nobody will show him. In 805 he is made a bishop against his wish and needs a boat up to Colonia and back.
stories.picture: An open grave field in wind: a tall priest saying Mass at a weathered wooden cross, the estate's people with their hoods up, a small new bell hanging from a pole between two posts, and at the back a Saxon woman with her lips moving.

beats.text: Liudger has bought the bend at Werden: good land, the ferryman says, and a bad landing. He wants a bell the height of a man's forearm from a founder at Colonia and glass for one window, and asks what a boat would charge to bring both without a crack.

On the river strip at Colonia a founder pours the bell in a pit behind the smiths' row, and Liutwin's glass men cut eight green panes. Erkanbert the old priest comes to hear the bell struck once and says a Saxon will walk a long way toward that sound, or away from it.

Liudger says Mass in the open at the old cross. Afterwards he asks, mildly, where the spring is that the old people say the place is named for. Nobody knows. Hathuswith, at the back, has said the Creed in Saxon and is looking at the ground under the hill.

At the end of March Liudger is consecrated bishop for the western Saxons by Archbishop Hildebold. He asked to be left with his monks and nobody heard him. A boat that brought him up the river is asked to take him back down it, and to say nothing of how he looked.

On the Ems, where the Frisians burned his churches in the year the game begins and had him back within a year, they hear that their priest is a bishop among the Saxons now. The blind singer Bernlef asks whether the new house on the Ruhr has a bell yet.
After Easter the bier goes up the Ruhr. If the bell reached Werden it is rung for him, the first time it has been rung for a death, and Wolfhelm at the pole says the fifth psalm right through.

endings.how: You brought the bell and the glass up the Ruhr whole, and carried the new bishop up to Colonia and back.
endings.text: Werden has a voice and one green window. The house is prayed for there by name, and the western Saxons learn that the bishop's boat is a Dorestad boat.
endings.reward: The thread's flag ms_carried_priest; the work diusburg.work.werden_bell reckoned as done; a bed at Werden; standing with the church from the Ruhr to the Ems; Liudger a fast friend until 809.

endings.how: You learned from the old people where the spring is, and told Liudger.
endings.text: He goes there alone, prays, and has a small cross cut and set over the water. Nothing is broken, because there is nothing there to break but a hollow and some rags. The old people stop leaving rags. They also stop telling a Frisian skipper things.
endings.reward: Liudger's thanks and his word for the house at Colonia and Traiectum; the estate's old people and the ferryman cool; Hathuswith says nothing and serves you last.

endings.how: You were shown the spring by Hathuswith or the ferryman, and kept it to yourself.
endings.text: Liudger asks once more and then lets it be. The hollow under the hill keeps its rags until the palace is built over it a hundred years on. Hathuswith tells you, for the first time, what she was called at home.
endings.reward: Hathuswith, Gerlind and Wolfhelm fast friends; the word of the Saxons on the Hellweg; nothing lost with Liudger, who never knows.

stories.reward: A bishop's friendship and a bed at Werden, or the trust of the people who were here before the priests, and in either case a bell on the Ruhr that the house paid to hear.

works.name: A strip of the king's bank
works.what: A boat's length of bank above the flood line, with a post-built shed and rollers of your own. It is held of the king's steward for an ounce of silver at Christmas, as the estate's tenants pay.
works.needs: The steward's good word: one cargo carried for the estate at the full count, or the finder's half honestly earned.
works.gives: Goods may be left here between voyages; the boat lies above the spring flood; porters cost nothing. It is what the ferry right asks for.
works.picture: A new shed of posts and thatch on the mud under the green hill, a barge on rollers beside it, the steward notching a tally stick and breaking it in two.
works.source: Each holding pays Prüm an ounce at Christmas (Prüm estate book of 893, ch. 97); the plot before the ferry in story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_ferry_barge. A merchant's plot in 793 is a guess (?)

works.name: A bell for Werden
works.what: A small cast bell for Liudger's new house up the Ruhr, with the cost of the founder at Colonia, the metal, and the carrying.
works.needs: Liudger met at the Ruhr mouth; a boat that can go up a shallow river, or Wolfhelm paid to take it.
works.gives: Standing with the church along the Rhine and in Frisia; a bed at Werden; the house prayed for by name; it counts toward the story of the books.
works.picture: A bell the height of a man's forearm slung from a pole between two monks wading ashore, a timber frame waiting for it against a line of oaks.
works.source: The spine's hook (cross_and_grove: Liudger 'wants books, a bell and glass'). Liudger asked for 'a bell' for the Frisians too (spine cast.liudger). The price and the founder at Colonia are guesses (?)

works.name: The market well
works.what: A well shaft lined with split oak, sunk in the wet ground of the new market so that sellers and beasts need not drink from the Rhine.
works.needs: The market begun (after 870); oak from the king's forest, which the steward sells.
works.gives: The market's people remember who paid: a better first price here, and fresher talk. It is the well that matters in the winter of 883.
works.picture: Men lowering a square frame of split oak into a hole in trodden ground, booths behind, a woman already waiting with two buckets.
works.source: The timber well at the Alter Markt, tree-ring dated 872 and later filled with burnt rubble (Krause, Wikinger I). That a merchant paid for it is invented

works.name: A house among the Frisians
works.what: A long house with a store and a boat shed in the row where the Frisians stay, held under the abbey of Prüm's hand. A man of yours can live there the year round.
works.needs: A Frisian here who will speak for you (Thiadward or his heirs), and your share of the abbot's silver paid at Martinmas and Easter.
works.gives: Room for 20 units of goods; free lodging; a factor here buys wine cheap after Martinmas and sends price word downriver. With the abbot's dues paid, no toll at this port.
works.picture: A row of long thatched houses end-on to the water, the newest with pale timbers, a scale hanging in the doorway and bales under tarred cloth.
works.source: The Frisians at Dusburhc (Prüm estate book of 893, ch. 97); story/works_793.json factor_house (cost and days from there; that table opens it in 793, the evidence here begins about 880-893)

works.name: The causeway to the gate
works.what: A made road of rubble and timber from the landing up to the palace gate, with a drain along one side and a small stone bridge over the wet place.
works.needs: The palace building (after 888); the king's steward's leave; a season when no court is expected.
works.gives: Loading and unloading take half the time in wet weather. When a king holds court here the house is among those asked to supply it.
works.picture: Labourers tipping baskets of stone between two lines of stakes across black mud, a little arched bridge half built, the grey ring of the palace above.
works.source: The causeway from the Rhine to the palace with a side drain and a small rubble-stone bridge, early 10th century (Krause, Königpfalz). A merchant's share in it is invented

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The boat of this bank: a flat plank barge of some sixteen metres, built of oak from the king's forest, caulked with moss under iron clamps, and towed back up by men on the path.
ships.picture: A long low box of a barge on rollers under the hill, flat raked ends, two men driving moss into a seam, a short towing mast lying beside her.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json (built_at includes diusburg); story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_river_barge (900 d); caulking clamps of the 9th to 13th century (Krause, Duisburger Hafen im Mittelalter)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The Ruhr boat: one long oak hollowed thin, spread with fire and water and raised by a plank a side. She goes up to Werden where a barge will not.
ships.picture: A long narrow dugout with one added plank a side, poled by a man standing in the stern, under overhanging alders.
ships.source: traffic_793.json (diusburg: river barges and expanded logboats); Design/content/ships.md

ships.note: Every holding on the bank has one for fishing and for the far shore. An old one can be had for a few pennies and a promise not to complain.
ships.picture: A short grey dugout half full of rainwater, tied to a stake, an eel trap in the bow.

ships.note: The abbeys' wine ships. Prüm's tenants upriver owe a trip with a ship twice a year to Saint Goar or to Diusburg; one lies here empty after Martinmas and can be hired down to the sea of reeds and back.
ships.picture: A twenty-metre oak barge with a heap of casks amidships landing bow-on to a sloping bank, a monk with a tablet counting.
ships.source: Prüm estate book of 893, ch. 69 'De Retersdorpht' (two ship services a year to St Goar or Duisburg); story/ships_793.json (built_at includes diusburg, from 826)

ships.how: held of the steward for a yearly render
ships.note: The crossing at the Ruhr mouth is the king's right, farmed to a man the steward trusts. When Wolfhelm's line fails it can be asked for.
ships.picture: A wide flat ferry with a cart and two oxen aboard, poled across brown water toward a gravel spit with a horn on a post.
ships.source: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_ferry_barge (lists diusburg; 300 d, by audience)

ships.how: built in spring from bought timber
ships.note: Oak from the king's forest between Rhine, Ruhr and Düssel comes down the Ruhr on the spring water and is lashed into rafts here for the yards downstream.
ships.picture: A raft of long oak trunks on the swollen Ruhr, four men with sweeps, a hut of bark on the middle of it.
ships.source: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_raft (lists diusburg); the forest in Lacomblet I no. 205 (1065)

sayings.text: A Frank laughs at a short cloak until he has to row in a long one.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, turning Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34, where Charles complains that the Frisians' short cloaks are no use in bed, on a horse or at stool

sayings.text: A hostage eats at the king's table and counts the doors.
The Rhine takes what he wants. The Ruhr only takes what you leave lying.
They fortified it in their usual way.
sayings.source: Regino of Prüm, Chronicon 884, 'more solito' (ed. Kurze 1890), translated here; said on this bank for a generation afterwards of anything done badly and at once (the use is invented)

sayings.text: At Diuspargum, which we commonly call Diusburg.
sayings.source: The emperor's clerk, 1 March 966 (Lacomblet I no. 109), translated here. A clerk's joke without meaning to be: he gives the landing the name of old King Chlodio's castle out of Gregory of Tours

sayings.text: I forsake the devil. And I forsake all the devil's works and words, Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot and all the fiends that are their companions.
sayings.source: The Old Saxon baptismal vow (Vatican, Pal. lat. 577, late 8th century), in the game's own English as it stands in texts_793.json saxon_vow (the first answer and the third); said by the hostages on the bank, and by the mate once

sayings.text: Ale is the same in every tongue. It is the reckoning that needs a translator.
A ship of Duisburg: a cake of wax and a pennyworth of wine. A ship of Cologne: four pennies and wine. So be from Duisburg.
sayings.source: The Koblenz toll list (Beyer, Mittelrheinisches Urkundenbuch I no. 409), mid 11th century; the last four words are invented

sayings.text: A church without books is a barn with a cross on it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, for Liudger

easter_eggs.text: In the summer of 810 the river is full of boats going down to Lippeham, a day downstream, where the emperor musters against Godfred. A boatman coming back up says the great grey beast from the east lay down there and died, and that it took forty men to bury it.
easter_eggs.source: chronicle_793.json 810-summer-elephant-dies (Annales regni Francorum 810); the spine's hook for godfreds_market. The forty men are invented

easter_eggs.text: Wolfhelm's pole strikes metal in mid-stream between the hill and the far bank: a bar of lead nearly as long as a man is tall, stamped with two letters, L and V. He thinks they are runes. They are the mark of the Fifth Legion, on the stock of a Roman anchor.
easter_eggs.source: Krause, Römische Ankerfunde aus dem Rhein bei Duisburg: a lead anchor stock, 1.36 m, about 150 kg, stamped L V, found between Duisburg and Homberg in 1968

easter_eggs.text: Over the river stand the broken walls of a Roman fort the boatmen call the ash burg. A monk going up to Werden says, with a straight face, that an old book in the abbey at Fulda has it founded by Ulysses on his way home.
easter_eggs.source: Tacitus, Germania 3: Asciburgium on the Rhine, said to be founded and named by Ulysses; the one manuscript lay at Hersfeld or Fulda in the 9th century (?). The monk is invented

easter_eggs.text: After about 830, a monk from up the Ruhr drinking at the ale-house says a brother of his house is putting the whole Gospel into Saxon verse, with Christ as a ring-giver and the apostles as his sworn men. Hathuswith's people would have understood every word.
easter_eggs.source: The Heliand, about 830; Werden is one of three houses proposed for it, with Fulda and Corvey (?)

easter_eggs.text: Among the books that go up the Ruhr in Liudger's years is one nobody at the ferry can read: silver letters on purple skin, in a tongue that is neither Latin nor Frankish. Liudger says only that it came over the mountains and should be kept dry.
easter_eggs.source: The Codex Argenteus, the Gothic gospels, was found at Werden in the 16th century; how it came there is not known, and that Liudger brought it from Italy is one guess among several (?)

easter_eggs.text: In the market of the 870s a porter carries two sacks where other men carry one. He is the tallest man on the Rhine, by a head. After the Northmen's winter there is a long grave by the burnt houses.
easter_eggs.source: Krause, Wikinger I and II: a hasty burial in the burn layer of 883/84, a man of about 40 and some 2 m tall. Tying the grave to that winter is Krause's reading; the porter is invented

easter_eggs.text: In May 945 a dead man comes to court. The clergy of Maastricht carry the body of Saint Servatius up to the king's hall to lay his complaint against Count Immo in person. The king hears him.

A penny struck here under the boy king Henry shows the Saviour's church from the water, above a wall: the view from the merchant's own boat. One like it goes into the ground on Sandoy in the Faroes about ten years after the game ends.
easter_eggs.source: Krause, Königpfalz (Henry IV's Duisburg pennies show a church twice, once from the water above a wall); en.wikipedia 'Sandur hoard' (a Duisburg coin; buried about 1070-80)

easter_eggs.text: The old people say the place is named for a god, Deuso, who had a holy spring under the hill. The priest says it is named for nothing of the kind. Nobody can show the spring.
easter_eggs.source: de.wikipedia 'Geschichte der Stadt Duisburg': one theory of the name, and only a theory

easter_eggs.text: Count Ezzo plays at the tables after dinner and, if he likes his guest, tells how he beat the young Emperor Otto three games running, the stake being whatever he chose, and chose the emperor's sister.
easter_eggs.source: The foundation legend of Brauweiler abbey (Fundatio monasterii Brunwilarensis), a legend and not history (?)

unlocks.what: word of where the mate's brother was sent
unlocks.how: Before 806, with Brunger in the crew: drink at Gerlind's, then speak with Hathuswith at the court kitchen.

unlocks.what: the Ruhr learned: the boat may go up to Werden without a pilot
unlocks.how: Hire Wolfhelm once at the Ruhr mouth and keep off the bar where he says, or carry Liudger's books (flag bk_carried).
unlocks.gives: flag diusburg_ruhr_water; no pilot's fee up the Ruhr; Werden's cellarer buys wine, wax and calfskin at the source price

unlocks.what: a standing order from Liudger's house at Werden for calfskin, wax and wine
unlocks.how: Carry the books up the Ruhr dry between 799 and 809, or bring a book to Werden in any year to 883.
unlocks.gives: flag bk_parchment; a yearly commission from Werden until the winter of 883

unlocks.what: the riddle of the thing that fights wave and wind
unlocks.how: Find the iron in the river with Wolfhelm, then ask at the ale-house on a riddle night.

unlocks.what: the riddle of the house that runs and the guest that is silent
unlocks.how: Carry a cargo up the Ruhr and come back down it in the same week.

unlocks.what: the crossing at the Ruhr mouth, held of the steward
unlocks.how: Hold the strip of bank (diusburg.work.plot), be trusted here, and ask at the court after 818, when Wolfhelm's line has no son at the pole.
unlocks.gives: the shared unlock unlock_ship_ferry_barge at this port

unlocks.what: Thiadward's bag under the burnt rubble of the market well
unlocks.how: Be shown the side of the well in the autumn of 883; come back after the thaw of 884 with men and a rope.

unlocks.what: to trade as one of the abbot of Prüm's protected men
unlocks.how: From 885: hold a house among the Frisians and pay the abbot's man your share at Martinmas and at Easter (the whole settlement owes 272 d a year).
unlocks.gives: toll none at Diusburg while the dues are paid; flag diusburg_prums_man; it lapses the first term a payment is missed

unlocks.what: to be counted a ship of Duisburg at the Koblenz toll
unlocks.how: From about 1050: hold a house or a plot here and lie here over one winter.
unlocks.gives: flag diusburg_home_ship; at the toll upriver the boat gives a cake of wax and a pennyworth of wine, not four pennies and wine

unlocks.what: a place among those who supply the king's court when it sits here
unlocks.how: Between 929 and 1016: pay for the causeway, or sell wine to the palace steward at a fair measure three times.
unlocks.gives: commission: in a year the king comes, wine, wax, fish and spices are bought from the house first and paid on the day

The editor's pass of 7 October 2026. Colonia lies above Diusburg on the Rhine and the Lippe's mouth below it, so the hostages, the steward's boy and the new bishop go up to Colonia, and Liudger's bier comes up from the north. The spur is about 8 m above the bank (dossier 1), which is five men's height. The vow is given as texts_793.json has it. Adalbert of Bremen fell in January 1066 (de.wikipedia 'Adalbert von Bremen'); what became of his gift is not known.
